title: The laziest sentence in ELT Wc9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoibmV3c2xldHRlciJ9fQ--45b49d2f1573025a3f783339d0d973f87fa 9055b4faacce7ccdf1af128e4c41d/preview
author: Cecilia Nobre
summary: Cecilia Nobre, an English language teacher educator, argues that the answer "it depends" is often the laziest sentence in the profession, because it hides the reasoning teachers need. Following a LinkedIn debate about "always" and "never" rules in teaching, she says that context does matter but that trainers owe teachers an explanation of which parts of the context matter and why. She illustrates with second language acquisition research on corrective feedback, including Li's meta-analysis and Lyster and Ranta's finding that prompts beat recasts for immediate uptake, and with Hu and Nation's work suggesting readers need roughly 98 percent lexical coverage. She then offers a three-question test for any teaching advice: when would I recommend this, what am I basing it on, and what would make me reconsider. She notes that firm rules feel safer during observation, but that making reasoning visible is how colleagues build judgement. The piece ends by asking readers which rule they would now qualify with a "when".
points: Saying "it depends" without naming the conditions is a shrug, and teacher educators owe teachers explicit reasoning about which context factors matter.
Research on corrective feedback and lexical coverage shows effects that vary by task and setting, so blanket rules such as "always correct" or "pre-teach every word" overreach.
The three-question test (when would I recommend this, what am I basing it on, what would make me reconsider) works on any advice, including the author's own.
The same questions can structure lesson feedback by asking trainees what influenced a decision and what might lead them to choose differently.
Firm rules feel safer under observation, but making reasoning visible is how teachers develop independent judgement.
quotes: Because “it depends” can be the laziest sentence in our profession. Of course context influences teaching. But which parts of the context? And why?
We owe teachers better answers than a shrug dressed up as professional wisdom
Li's (2010) meta-analysis found that corrective feedback generally benefits language learning. The effects were stronger in laboratory studies than in classroom studies.
Their findings suggest that readers need to know around 98% of the words in a text for adequate comprehension under the conditions they studied.
When would I recommend this? Think about the learners, learning aims and task conditions.
What would make me reconsider? What would I need to observe before trying another approach?
It's easier to cite a rule during feedback than explain a judgement call made under pressure
But when we train or advise teachers, we should make that reasoning visible. That's how colleagues develop the judgement to make informed decisions for themselves.
